name: Mogging as TikTok fitness trend

lead: Mogging is slang for outshining another person in appearance, and on TikTok it shows up in fitness and bodybuilding videos that compare physiques, frames and faces.
Creators use the label to promote gym training and grooming, while commentators debate whether it motivates viewers or fuels appearance anxiety.

paras: Viewers encounter short videos of physique comparisons and transformations and may adopt the gym, diet or grooming routines shown. The milder end of looksmaxxing, called softmaxxing, includes exercise and weight management.

Researchers cited in Wikipedia see encouragement of fitness as potentially positive but describe the broader practice as demoralizing, especially for young men. Harder practices sometimes promoted alongside it carry documented health risks.

chain: Watch mogging comparison and transformation videos
Adopt the gym and grooming habits shown
More muscle and a more polished look
angle.text: The trend works as motivation content: physique comparisons point viewers toward lifting, diet and grooming habits that change how they look.

lead: Mogging is slang, described by Wikipedia as originating in incel-linked circles, for asserting dominance over another person based on appearance [1]. On TikTok, mostly male creators popularized looksmaxxing content in the 2020s, including physique and frame comparisons in fitness and bodybuilding video [1].

For viewers the appearance payoff is practical: the videos advertise gym training, leaner body composition and grooming as ways to look better. Gym use and general fitness are classed as softmaxxing, the milder end of the practice [1].

Coverage by outlets such as the BBC, The New York Times and The Guardian has discussed the trend, and researchers have said its encouragement of health and fitness may be positive while the practice overall is demoralizing for many young men [1].

paras: On TikTok, early looksmaxxing content often framed itself as self-improvement, sometimes with self-deprecating humor [1]. Mogging clips in fitness circles extend this by comparing bodies and faces.

Halpin and colleagues (2025) are cited as seeing health and fitness encouragement as potentially positive while finding the practice demoralizing overall for young men [1]. A Conversation article argued TikTok algorithms can steer young men toward incel content [1].
